Lessons.Title: Find Missing Side Lengths
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 G5 U04:L15 Find Missing Side Lengths connects multiplication and division to area in SQUARE feet and prism volume in CUBIC feet. Learners must identify which dimension is missing, choose the correct divisor (side versus base area) and recognize insufficient data when TWO side lengths are unknown.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration The Garden: original source garden photograph with third-party Pixabay credit is not copied; pupils supply too low/about right/too high estimates and explain visual uncertainty. The photograph alone does not yield a single exact area.

Activity 1 Find the Missing Side Length Part1 original rectangle TABLE in feet: area816 sq ft and length24 ft gives width34; area1248 sq ft and WIDTH48 ft gives length26; length23 ft and width253 ft gives missing area5819 sq ft; area5796 sq ft and width36 ft gives length161. Preserve area units and avoid swapping table columns, which were independently verified from original HTML cell markup.

Activity 2 Part2 original volume/base-area TABLE: volume375 cubic ft, base area15 square ft gives height25 ft; volume1176 cubic ft and height28 ft gives base area42 square ft. Clare's source prism has volume882 cubic ft, length6 ft, width7 ft, so base area42 square ft and height21 ft; her first step 882÷6=147 must then be divided by the other width7.

Same Activity2 later prism TABLE: volume936 cubic ft, length8 ft, height9 ft -> missing width13 ft; volume1536 cubic ft, WIDTH48 ft, height2 ft -> missing length16 ft; volume1008 cubic ft, LENGTH36 ft, width and height both missing -> only their PRODUCT is 1008÷36=28 square feet. Valid pairs such as 4×7 and2×14 illustrate that the individual dimensions are NOT uniquely determined, and teacher reviews explanation.

Exact numerical Practice only checks bounded source entries and product28, explicitly without pretending width/height unique. Original diagrams/photograph, student explanations and distinct valid dimensions require TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED; independent Cool-down is Edulytiks-authored.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing rectangle side
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing area by one known perpendicular side yields the other linear dimension.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing prism height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing volume by its known base area yields corresponding linear height.

KeyConcepts.Title: Not always one answer
KeyConcepts.Definition: Knowing volume and only ONE edge leaves the product of two missing edges, not each edge individually.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 960 ft³÷32 ft=30 ft², with several factor pairs.

Steps: 23×253=5819 square ft missing area; 5796÷36=161 ft missing length.

WorkedExamples.Method: Divide by product of all known dimensions, and flag underdetermined cases.

WorkedExamples.Answer: 13 ft width;16 ft length; width×height=28 sq ft (no unique pair).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Report square feet as a missing side length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area divided by a linear side yields a linear measurement.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Select one arbitrary factor pair as the only remaining prism dimensions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One known edge and volume determine only the product of the two remaining edges.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Supply several valid factorizations or ask for another dimension.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat made-up 1536 sq ft/48 ft lawn and 2160 cu ft/base120 prism as the original textbook's only values
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Printed source has multiple exact table cells, with an intentional last underdetermined 1008 cu ft prism.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore all original table rows with correct column placements, distinguish square vs cubic units and record ambiguous last row.

SummaryPoints: Source volume/base table: 375/15=25 ft height,1176/28=42 sq ft base.
Clare's 882/(6×7)=21 ft height; source 936/(8×9)=13 ft width,1536/(48×2)=16 ft length.
Source 1008 cu ft and length36 means width×height=28 square ft; infinitely many positive pairs, no single width.
Teacher reviews source photo, units and underdetermined geometry; selected digital answers exclude freehand explanation.

Lessons.Title: World’s Record Noodle Soup
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L16 World’s Record Noodle Soup has a Chinese food company with a Guinness-record single continuous noodle approximately TEN THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED NINETEEN FEET long (10119 ft), equally shared among FOUR HUNDRED people (400). The source fraction remaining after division must be allocated fairly; neither treating the length as an unrelated piece count nor discarding remainder matches the task.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder World Record Event: original source describes the approximately10119-foot longest noodle. Pupils explain physical scale and what length in FEET means. Source photo/media not reproduced and length is approximate in the real world while source arithmetic treats the stated 10119 as the modeled whole.

Activity 1 How Many Feet in One Serving? 10119÷400. Reason with 400×25=10000, slightly BELOW total10119; everyone receives MORE than25 feet. Exactly in the mathematical model, after25 whole feet each, 119 feet remain to share among400: share is 25+119/400 feet =25.2975 feet per person. Students estimate before full calculation and decide if their estimate is lower or higher with source inequalities.

Activity 2 Han's Estimate: Han says each person will get about 25 1/4 feet (25.25). For400 people his claim corresponds to 400×(25+1/4)=10100ft, only19ft short of the modeled10119; exact share exceeds Han's estimate by 19/400ft (0.0475ft) per person. His estimate is reasonable, slightly low; teacher reviews explanation instead of an unverified publisher answer key.

Exact digital Practice validates bounded INTEGER subskills such as the 25 whole feet per person,119 leftover feet,10000 baseline,10100 Han total and19 aggregate difference. These are NOT claimed to be the full fractional share; the mixed-number 25 119/400, visual fair sharing, real-world context and qualitative estimation remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Earlier 2050÷80=25 5/8 remains an optional correct extension only. Edulytiks authored independent Cool-down shares8011ft among400.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Division with remainder as fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: When a length is shared equally and remainder remains, divide it as well.

KeyConcepts.Title: Continuous noodle length
KeyConcepts.Definition: The length of one object can be partitioned into equal portions without treating the fraction as new whole noodles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every share multiplied by diner count reconstructs original length.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed total with more recipients
KeyConcepts.Definition: More equal shares from a fixed positive total yield smaller share lengths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original record noodle source fractional share
WorkedExamples.Question: A 10119-foot noodle is shared equally by400 diners. How many feet per person?
WorkedExamples.Method: Whole-number quotient and leftover part divided by all people.
Steps: 400×25=10000 feet are allocated as25 feet to each diner.
Original modeled length minus that is119 feet left.
Each receives an additional 119/400 foot; no noodle discarded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Han about25 and one quarter
WorkedExamples.Question: How does Han's 25¼ foot estimate per diner compare to exact mathematical share?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply his estimated share by total diners and compare to source total.
Steps: Per person Han underestimates by19/400 feet.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Reasonable but slightly low; true modeled share is25 119/400 feet.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate without completing source division
WorkedExamples.Question: Is25 feet per person above or below 10119÷400?
Steps: Equal share therefore exceeds25 feet per diner.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 25 feet is lower than the exact share.
WorkedExamples.Check: Bounded reasoning without calculating full quotient.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Find a mixed quotient
WorkedExamples.Question: 2050 feet of noodle among80 diners. Length per person?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party context model with exact multiplication or fraction-quotient inverse check.
Steps: 50 feet remain, shared equally as50/80 feet each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Change diner count
WorkedExamples.Question: If the same 2050-foot noodle is shared among100 diners, what is the share?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party context model with exact multiplication or fraction-quotient inverse check.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Check a wrong remainder interpretation
WorkedExamples.Question: A student says each diner gets25 feet, while50 extra feet should simply be thrown away. Explain the error.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party context model with exact multiplication or fraction-quotient inverse check.
Steps: Identify leftover50 feet from the whole.
The sharing goal is equal division of the entire single noodle.
Give each diner50/80 feet beyond the25 feet.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Each gets25 5/8 feet; no length is unaccounted for.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies the meaning of the fraction from the fixed continuous original.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignore the remainder in exact equal sharing
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The continuous noodle has length beyond the whole-number partial share.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Represent remainder divided by recipient count as a fractional length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Read the quotient remainder as extra whole people
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The remainder is measured in feet, not in number of diners.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label every intermediate quantity in its proper units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Substitute fabricated original noodle 2050ft/80 diners and discard continuous length remainder
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source original specifies approx10119ft and400 diners, whose fractional remainder119/400 differs substantially.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore10119÷400, use25 whole feet plus119/400, and compare directly to Han's25¼ estimate.

SummaryPoints: Original source record: one noodle approximately10119 feet long, serving400 people.
Han's about25 1/4 foot share is slightly low by19/400 ft/person.
Selected Practice only checks integer components; fractional sharing model and estimates are teacher reviewed.
Prior 2050ft/80 example remains optional extension and is NOT original source.

Lessons.Title: Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM 2021 Grade5 U04:L17 Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional) asks students to recognize that a quotient may be represented as a fraction and as a SUM of fractions with the SAME denominator. A correct full quotient requires all numerators collectively to equal the source dividend; not all individual partial fractions need integer values.
Warm-up What Do You Know About 60/6+6/6?: original sum10+1=11, equal 66/6. Teacher asks students to notice numerator partitioning and explain why shared denominator6 is preserved.

Activity 1 Select Expressions: original target 78/6=13. VALID source options are 78÷6;66/6+12/6;60/6+18/6;and(60÷6)+(18÷6). INVALID are77/6+8/6=85/6 and(60÷6)+18=28. Students must select ALL true representations, defend rejection of close distractors, and show why sum of numerators corresponds to78, not merely choose one correct number.

Activity 2 Choose One Expression: all three printed source decompositions of165÷15=11 are valid:75/15+80/15+10/15, (30+30+30+60+15)/15 and150/15+15/15. The first includes 80/15, not an integer quotient, and is still a valid fraction sum; do not falsely disqualify it. For540÷18=30 the valid printed options include180/18+180/18+180/18,500/18+40/18,and360/18+180/18. Pupils compare helpfulness of decompositions and explain their choices.

Original fraction-sum selection, source expression validity, partner proof and explanation of noninteger partial chunks remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Existing 84÷7 first-party examples are correct but OPTIONAL EXTENSIONS, not source tasks. The exact digital family supports only integer-valued source subproblems and targets; it is not certified to grade open source fraction-sum sets. Independent Edulytiks Cool-down uses96÷8.

Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: A fraction is division
KeyConcepts.Definition: The fraction numerator divided by denominator expresses the exact quotient.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient fractions add
KeyConcepts.Definition: Splitting the numerator into parts and dividing each by the SAME divisor preserves value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check an entire expression
KeyConcepts.Definition: A candidate sum may contain valid fractions yet not equal the target quotient.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Numerators must total the original dividend when denominators are the same.

WorkedExamples.Method: Conserve numerator total across common denominator and evaluate grouping.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Four valid source choices; reject two distractors.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks select-all classification and explanation.

WorkedExamples.Method: Any sum with denominator15 and numerator total165 is equivalent.
Steps: 75+80+10=165, even if 80/15 is not an integer.
WorkedExamples.Check: Partial fractions do not need integer values.

WorkedExamples.Method: Choose numerator decompositions and evaluate whole quotient.

WorkedExamples.Method: First-party context model with exact multiplication or fraction-quotient inverse check.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The first three are equivalent; the last is not.

Steps: Compare which partial calculations are convenient.

Steps: Compare with84÷7=12 and locate the missing division by7.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add a numerator not divided by the same divisor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The decomposition must distribute the division across EVERY numerator part.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep /7 on both parts when splitting84/7.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat any two true quotient expressions as a correct matching pair
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Correctly computed individual fractions may sum to a different total.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add numerator contributions and compare with original dividend before accepting.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use invented84/7 rather than source78/6 and falsely reject80/15 as a noninteger partial quotient
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source explicitly demonstrates fraction sums whose individual numerators need not be divisible by the common denominator.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore source78/6,165/15,540/18 and explain conservation of summed numerators including noninteger parts.

SummaryPoints: Original 78/6 select-all: first four listed expressions valid, last two invalid.
Source165÷15=11 with three valid decompositions, even noninteger individual fractions.
Source540÷18=30 with three printed valid fraction-sum forms.
Teacher reviews original select-all, fraction sums and helpfulness reasoning; fixed digital exact cases only supplement.
